claim: DOJ's November 2024 proposed remedies package included a specific ban on third-party payments for pre-installation of Google search on non-Google devices, which the court rejected.
stance_target: the payment ban scenario was live/considered but ultimately not adopted
quoted_support: Third-party payments ban: Banning payments for pre-installation of Google search on non-Google devices

claim: The court explicitly reasoned that banning third-party default-search payments would risk harming distribution partners (particularly smaller firms) and consumers who benefit from Google's services -- the stated rationale for permitting continued Apple payments.
stance_target: why the payment ban was rejected
quoted_support: Third-party payments permitted: Google may continue paying distributors such as Apple or Samsung to set Google as the default search engine. The court reasoned that banning such payments would risk harming distribution partners -- particularly smaller firms -- and consumers who benefit from Google's services.

claim: EU evidence on mandatory Android choice screens shows only marginal effect on consumer switching behavior: 97% of users still selected Google as default even after being shown a choice screen.
stance_target: structural/behavioral remedies (choice screens, exclusivity bans) yield limited real-world erosion of Google's default position
quoted_support: Evidence from the European Union -- where the European Commission went further by requiring choice screens on Android devices -- indicates that such measures have little effect on behavior, with 97% of users still selecting Google.

claim: Google's stock price rose nearly 8% on September 2, 2025, the day the remedies ruling was issued, reflecting market interpretation of the outcome as a win for Google (and by extension, favorable for Apple's continued TAC revenue).
stance_target: market pricing treats the remedy as favorable/non-disruptive to the Google-Apple payment arrangement
quoted_support: Markets quickly interpreted the outcome as a win for Google, with its share price rising by nearly 8% after the decision.

claim: Data-sharing remedy requires a one-time snapshot of Google's search index plus ongoing but privacy-filtered ('k-anonymization, noise injection, generalization') disclosure of user-interaction data to qualified competitors, overseen by a court-appointed Technical Committee, with advertising/advertiser data carved out entirely.
stance_target: precise scope of the data-sharing remedy
quoted_support: The judgment imposes two data-sharing obligations: Google must provide a one-time snapshot of its search index to qualified competitors, and it must also disclose certain "user-interaction" data -- covering queries, clicks, and dwell times -- on an ongoing basis... The court itself acknowledged these risks and therefore conditioned disclosure on privacy-enhancing techniques, including k-anonymization, noise injection, and generalization.
